ggdemetra3: extending ggplot2 to perform seasonal adjustment with rjdverse packages

Alain Quartier-la-Tente

2026-10-28

Source: vignettes/ggdemetra3.Rmd
ggdemetra3.Rmd

ggdemetra3 is an extension of ggplot2 to add seasonal adjustment statistics to your plots.
The seasonal adjustment process is performed using the R packages associated with version 3 of JDemetra+, which is the seasonal adjustment software officially recommended for members of the European Statistical System (ESS) and the European System of Central Banks.
rjd3x13 is used for X-13, rjd3tramoseats for TRAMO-SEATS, and rjd3highfreq for high-frequency seasonal adjustment methods. In addition, ggdemetra3 provides functions to visualize linear filters, weights, and trend-cycle estimation tools from the rjd3filters infrastructure.

Note that ts objects cannot be directly used in ggplot2. To convert ts or mts objects to a data.frame, you can use the ts2df() function. For example, the data ipi_c_eu_df used in this package is obtained by applying the ts2df() function to ipi_c_eu:

ipi_c_eu_df <- ts2df(ipi_c_eu)

Seasonal adjustment specification

All the functions share some common parameters, especially those defining the seasonal adjustment method:

  • method is the method used for the seasonal adjustment: X-13ARIMA (method = "x13", the default) or TRAMO-SEATS (method = "tramoseats").
  • spec is the seasonal adjustment specification. It can be the name of a pre-defined specification (see ?rjd3x13::x13 or ?rjd3tramoseats::tramoseats) or a user-defined specification.
  • frequency is the frequency of the input time series. By default, the frequency is computed automatically and a message is printed with the chosen value (use message = FALSE to suppress this message).

In the following examples, the data used is the French industrial production index.
By default, the seasonal adjustment is processed with X-13ARIMA using the pre-defined specification "rsa3" (automatic log detection, automatic ARIMA and outlier detection, trading day, and Easter adjustment).
However, for industrial production, working day effects have more economic sense than trading day effects, and a gradual Easter effect is less appropriate for aggregated series.
The recommended specification to use with X-13ARIMA in this case is spec = rjd3toolkit::set_tradingdays(rjd3x13::spec_x13("rsa3"), option = "workingdays").
If no new data or seasonal adjustment specification (method or spec) is provided, these parameters are inherited from the previous call: therefore, you only need to specify them once.

library(ggplot2)
library(ggdemetra3)
p_ipi_fr <- ggplot(data = ipi_c_eu_df, mapping = aes(x = date, y = FR)) +
    geom_line() +
    labs(title = "Seasonal adjustment of the French industrial production index",
         x = NULL, y = NULL)
p_ipi_fr

Add the result of the seasonal adjustment

By default, geom_sa() adds the seasonally adjusted time series:

spec <- rjd3x13::spec_x13("rsa3")
spec <- rjd3toolkit::set_tradingdays(spec, option = "WorkingDays")
p_ipi_fr +
    geom_sa(color = "red",
            spec = spec)
#> Frequency used: 12

To add other components of the seasonal adjustment, use the component parameter of geom_sa() (see ?rjd3x13::userdefined_variables_x13() or ?rjd3tramoseats::userdefined_variables_tramoseats() for the available parameters). For example, to add the forecasts of the input data and of the seasonally adjusted series:

p_sa <- p_ipi_fr +
    geom_sa(component = "y_f(12)", linetype = 2, message = FALSE,
            spec = spec) + 
    geom_sa(component = "sa", color = "red") +
    geom_sa(component = "sa_f", color = "red", linetype = 2)
p_sa

Add the outliers to the plot

There are four different geometries to add the names of the outliers used in the pre-adjustment process to the plot:

  • geom = "text" (the default) adds directly the names of the outliers, and geom = "label" draws a rectangle behind the names, making them easier to read.
  • geom = "text_repel" and geom = "label_repel" do the same, but text labels repel away from each other and away from the data points (see ?ggrepel::geom_label_repel).

In our example, there are 3 outliers:

p_sa + geom_outlier(geom = "label")

They can be plotted in a more readable way using the parameters of ggrepel::geom_label_repel:

p_sa + 
    geom_outlier(geom = "label_repel",
                 ylim = c(NA, 65), force = 10,
                 arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.03, "npc"),
                               type = "closed", ends = "last"))

Use the parameters first_date and last_date to restrict the plotted outliers to a precise time interval. For example, to only plot outliers from 2009 onwards, use first_date = 2009:

p_sa + 
    geom_outlier(geom = "label_repel",
                 first_date = 2009,
                 ylim = c(NA, 65), force = 10,
                 arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.03, "npc"),
                               type = "closed", ends = "last"))

Add the ARIMA model

The ARIMA model used in the pre-adjustment process can be added to the plot with geom_arima(). The parameter geom = "label" draws a rectangle behind the ARIMA model, making it easier to read:

p_sa + 
    geom_arima(geom = "label",
               x_arima = -Inf, y_arima = -Inf, 
               vjust = -1, hjust = -0.1)

Add a table with some diagnostics

A table with diagnostics on the seasonal adjustment process can be added using geom_diagnostics(). The desired diagnostics must be passed to the diagnostics parameter (see ?rjd3x13::userdefined_variables_x13() or ?rjd3tramoseats::userdefined_variables_tramoseats() for available diagnostics). For example, to add the X-11 Q-M2 statistic and the p-values of the residual seasonality QS and F-tests:

diagnostics <- c("m-statistics.q-m2",
                 "diagnostics.seas-sa-qs",
                 "diagnostics.seas-sa-f")
p_sa + 
    geom_diagnostics(diagnostics = diagnostics,
                     ymin = 58, ymax = 72, xmin = 2010,
                     table_theme = gridExtra::ttheme_default(base_size = 8))

To customize the names of the diagnostics in the plot, pass a named vector to the diagnostics parameter:

diagnostics <- c(`Q-M2` = "m-statistics.q-m2",
                 `Residual qs-test (p-value)` = "diagnostics.seas-sa-qs",
                 `Residual f-test (p-value)` = "diagnostics.seas-sa-f")
p_sa + 
    geom_diagnostics(diagnostics = diagnostics,
                     ymin = 58, ymax = 72, xmin = 2010,
                     table_theme = gridExtra::ttheme_default(base_size = 8))

To place the table below the plot, you can use gridExtra::grid.arrange():

p_diag <- ggplot(data = ipi_c_eu_df, mapping = aes(x = date, y = FR))  +
    geom_diagnostics(diagnostics = diagnostics,
                     spec = spec,
                     table_theme = gridExtra::ttheme_default(base_size = 8),
                     message = FALSE) + 
    theme_void()
    
gridExtra::grid.arrange(p_sa, p_diag,
    nrow = 2, heights = c(4, 1.5))

Plot models

The autoplot() function also allows plotting an already estimated seasonal adjustment model.
The components parameter allows specifying which components to display:

mod <- rjd3x13::x13(ipi_c_eu[,"FR"],"rsa3")
autoplot(mod, components = c("y", "sa", "trend" = "t"))

autoplot(mod, components = c("seasonal" = "s", "irregular" = "i"))

High-frequency seasonal adjustment (rjd3highfreq)

ggdemetra3 also supports high-frequency seasonal adjustment methods provided by the rjd3highfreq package (such as fractional airline decomposition, X11-extended, STL, etc.).

For instance, you can decompose high-frequency weekly data (like usclaims) using geom_sa() with method = "fractionalairline" and setting frequency = 52:

p_usclaims <- ggplot(data = usclaims[usclaims$date <= "2019-12-01", ], 
                     mapping = aes(x = date, y = `Initial claims`)) +
    geom_line() +
    labs(title = "Initial claims (weekly data)", x = NULL, y = NULL)

p_usclaims + 
    geom_sa(method = "fractionalairline", frequency = 52, 
            component = "sa", color = "red", message = FALSE)

Alternatively, you can compute a decomposition object directly using rjd3highfreq and visualize it with autoplot():

mod_hf <- rjd3highfreq::fractional_airline_decomposition(
    usclaims[usclaims$date <= "2019-12-01", "Initial claims"], 
    period = 52
)
autoplot(mod_hf, dates = usclaims$date[usclaims$date <= "2019-12-01"])
